subsection: 1. Nutritional significance and structure of meat

points: Red meat: beef, lamb, pork and veal.
Poultry: chicken, turkey and duck; the breast is paler than the leg because it contains less myoglobin.
Offal: edible organs such as liver, kidney and heart; liver is the richest source of several vitamins and iron among the offal.

notes.b: Meat is valued mainly for its protein, haem iron and B group vitamins, and it contributes little carbohydrate to the diet.
points: Protein: meat is a high biological value (HBV) protein source, supplying all the essential amino acids in the proportions the body needs.
Meat supplies about 20 to 30 per cent protein by weight.
Protein supplies amino acids for growth and repair of body cells and for making enzymes, hormones and antibodies.
Fat: meat fat is mainly saturated; it supplies energy and insulation, and its amount depends on the animal, the cut and whether visible fat is removed.
Carbohydrate: meat contains no carbohydrate, so it should be served with a starchy food such as potatoes, pasta or bread.
Haem iron: red meat, poultry and offal contain haem iron, which the body absorbs more readily than non-haem iron from plant foods.
Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood.
Zinc supports enzyme activity, potassium supports muscle function, and phosphorus supports bones, teeth and energy release.
B group vitamins help the body release energy from food; cobalamin (B12) is found naturally only in animal foods.
Vitamin A and vitamin D are found mainly in liver; meat contains no vitamin C.
Water makes up about 50 to 60 per cent of meat, and extractives released during cooking give meat its flavour.
Protein from meat supports growth in children and teenagers and repair of tissue in adults.
People with coronary heart disease should limit saturated fat and cholesterol, so lean cuts are chosen and visible fat is trimmed.
Haem iron is especially important for pregnant women, menstruating women, children and teenagers, to prevent iron-deficiency anaemia.
Tough or overcooked meat is harder to digest, so tender cuts cooked gently suit older people and anyone with a poor appetite.
Department of Health healthy eating guidelines advise limiting processed meats because of their salt and saturated fat content.
The Irish Food Pyramid places meat, fish, eggs and beans in one food group, with lean and unprocessed choices recommended.
Muscle is made of bundles of long, thin fibres, each fibre being a single muscle cell, running in the direction of the pull.
Fibres are grouped into bundles, which are held together by connective tissue.
Each fibre contains myofibrils made of the proteins actin and myosin; these slide past each other to shorten the muscle.
Connective tissue holds the muscle together and attaches it to bone; it contains collagen and elastin.
Fat is found as marbling within the muscle, as a layer under the skin, and around the organs; marbling adds juiciness and flavour.
Myosin and actin are the contractile proteins of the myofibrils and make up most of the muscle fibre.
Myoglobin is the oxygen-carrying pigment of muscle and gives raw meat its red colour; it turns brown or grey when heated.
Globulin is a soluble protein of the muscle fluid and is lost into cooking juices.
Collagen is an insoluble protein that forms tough connective tissue; it converts to gelatine when heated slowly in moisture.
Elastin is a springy connective tissue protein in tendons and ligaments; cooking does not soften it.

keyTerms.definition: The edible organs of an animal, such as liver, kidney and heart.
A protein that contains all the essential amino acids in the proportions the body needs.
Iron found in animal foods, absorbed by the body more readily than the non-haem iron in plant foods.
A thread-like structure within a muscle fibre, made of actin and myosin, that contracts to shorten the muscle.
A thick contractile protein in myofibrils that works with actin to shorten the muscle.
A thin contractile protein in myofibrils that slides along myosin during muscle contraction.
A tough, insoluble connective tissue protein that converts to gelatine when cooked slowly in moisture.
A springy connective tissue protein found in tendons and ligaments that is not softened by cooking.
The red, oxygen-storing pigment in muscle that gives raw meat its colour.
Fat deposits lying within the muscle, which give meat juiciness and flavour.

factCards.term: Four functions of protein in the body
factCards.definition: Growth, repair of body cells, making enzymes and hormones, and making antibodies for immunity.

factCards.term: Three nutrients meat supplies in valuable amounts
factCards.definition: Haem iron, cobalamin (vitamin B12) and high biological value protein.

factCards.term: Two vitamins found mainly in liver

factCards.definition: Collagen, which becomes gelatine when cooked slowly in moisture, and elastin, which cooking does not soften.

questions.prompt: Name two proteins found in meat and state two functions of protein in the body.
questions.model: Any two proteins named, one mark each: myosin, actin, globulin, collagen, elastin or myoglobin. Two functions, one mark each: growth; repair of body cells; making enzymes; making hormones; making antibodies. Credit a function linked to the named protein, such as myosin and actin enabling muscle contraction for movement.

questions.prompt: Give an account of the nutritional significance of meat in the diet, referring to protein, fat, carbohydrate, minerals and vitamins.
questions.model: Protein: HBV protein supplying all essential amino acids; about 20 to 30 per cent of meat; needed for growth, repair, enzymes and hormones. Fat: mainly saturated; energy and insulation; amount varies with animal, cut and cooking method; limit for coronary heart disease. Carbohydrate: none, so serve with potatoes, pasta or bread. Minerals: haem iron in red meat, poultry and offal for haemoglobin and preventing anaemia; zinc for enzyme activity; potassium for muscle function; phosphorus for bones and energy release. Vitamins: B group vitamins for releasing energy from food; B12 found only in animal foods; vitamins A and D in liver; no vitamin C. Dietetic note: needs for growing children, pregnant women and teenagers; processed meats high in salt and saturated fat.
